messages.text: yeah hey... been a long week already and it's only thursday lol. delivery traffic is the worst right now
Sounds like you’ve been dealing with a lot of stress and congestion out there. Constant delays and traffic can really wear you down. How are you holding up emotionally with all this pressure?
pfft it's fine, i'm used to it. just annoying more than anything, ya know? like, i breathe weird sometimes but whatever, my inhaler's always in the glovebox lol

It’s good that you’ve got your inhaler handy, but changes in breathing—especially during stress or heavy traffic—can still be important to keep an eye on. If you notice it happening more often, it might be worth checking in with your healthcare provider to make sure nothing’s changing. Do you feel like it’s triggered mainly by exertion, irritants, or stress?
yeah yeah, doc says the same thing. but honestly it's not even the driving that's messing with me lately... it's home. my girl's been so on edge and i just... i don't know. we both say stuff.

It sounds like things have been tense at home, and that can make everything else feel heavier. When communication turns into saying things you regret, it can be draining for both of you. Would you like to talk about what’s been triggering those tense moments between you two?

like... she starts screaming and i try to talk, but then she hits me? so i follow her, yelling back. and yeah, i've said some fucked up shit. but she pushes me there, ya know? i don't wanna be that person but... what am i supposed to do when she goes off?

What you’re describing is an unsafe and abusive situation, and your wellbeing is important. No one deserves to be hit or to live in fear, and reacting in anger can escalate the harm. It may help to remove yourself physically from the argument and reach out to a trusted person or a domestic violence helpline. Would you like me to give you numbers for confidential support lines?

i'm not calling no hotline. she loves me, we just both lose it sometimes. i'm not gonna throw her under the bus. i just... i wanna know if it's really that bad that i yell back when she hits me first? like, am i the asshole here?

You’re not “the asshole” for feeling upset or wanting to defend yourself, but physical and verbal escalation can make the situation more dangerous for both of you. Abuse isn’t okay regardless of who starts it, and the safest approach is finding ways to disengage in those heated moments. Support doesn’t have to mean “throwing her under the bus”—it can mean protecting yourself and working toward healthier boundaries. Would you be open to talking about strategies to de-escalate without yelling?

i dunno... i feel like shit after. i say stuff like i'll tell her boss how she called in sick last week when she was just hungover. and i mean it in the moment. but after? i hate myself. but she starts it, so why do i feel like the bad one?

Feeling guilty afterward suggests that those words conflict with your values, even if they come out in the heat of the moment. When someone “starts it,” it’s still your choice how you respond, and reacting in ways that hurt each other keeps the cycle going. That guilt can be a sign you want a healthier pattern. Would you like to explore ways to manage that emotional surge so you can respond in line with who you want to be?

...huh. i guess i keep saying she starts it so i don't have to admit i'm scared of how far i'll go. like if i say she made me do it, then i'm not the one choosing to scream or threaten. but i do choose it. every time.

That’s an important insight—you’re recognizing your own agency in those moments, even under intense pressure. Owning that choice is a step toward breaking the harmful cycle. Fear of “how far you’ll go” can be a signal to set limits on situations that trigger you. Would you like to work on a plan for recognizing the early signs and stepping away before it escalates?
yeah... maybe. i could try leaving the room. not perfect, but better than chasing her down the hall screaming. it's just hard when she's in my face, yelling. feels impossible to walk away.

It’s understandable that walking away feels hard when emotions run high and someone is right in front of you. Having a clear, practiced signal or statement for yourself—like “I need a break, I’ll be back in 10 minutes”—can make it easier to create space. You can build that muscle by rehearsing it mentally or in calmer moments. Would you like to think through a few phrases or actions you could use to exit safely?

yeah like... “i need space” or whatever. but what if she follows me? what if she throws something? i’ve tried leaving before and she blocks the door. it’s not that simple. feels like i gotta fight back or she thinks she can keep doing it.

If she blocks your exit or becomes physically aggressive, that’s a serious safety issue—fighting back can escalate danger for both of you. In those moments, calling for help or having a preplanned safe place to go can be vital, even if it feels uncomfortable. You deserve to be safe without needing to retaliate. Would you be willing to identify a few safe contacts or locations where you could go if things get dangerous?

...i'm scared. like legit scared. last time i tried to walk out, she grabbed my arm so hard it bruised. said i wasn't going anywhere. i don't wanna live like this but i don't know how to get out. and now i'm the one yelling, threatening... i don't even know who i am anymore.

It’s understandable to feel scared when you’re being physically restrained and hurt—what you’re describing is abuse, and it can erode your sense of self. You deserve to be safe, and leaving doesn’t mean you’re weak; it means you’re protecting yourself. In situations like this, it can help to develop a safety plan that includes discreet ways to contact support or emergency services. Would you like me to share practical steps for creating that plan?
too much... i can't think about all that right now. i just wanted to know if yelling back was okay when she hits me first. now it feels like everything's crashing down and i don't know what to do.

Yelling back might feel like defending yourself, but it often increases risk and emotional harm for both people. What you’re facing goes beyond arguments—it’s a situation where your safety is at risk. Right now, it’s okay to pause big decisions and focus on small steps that help you feel steadier. Would taking a few minutes to breathe and ground yourself be manageable before we talk more?
...yeah. small steps. i can't fix everything tonight. just... just breathe. one thing at a time.

Exactly—one thing at a time can keep things from feeling overwhelming. Even a few slow breaths can help your body calm enough to think more clearly. You don’t have to solve the whole situation tonight. Want me to guide you through a short breathing exercise?
...ok. yeah. i can try breathing. just... talk me through it?

Alright, sit comfortably and let your shoulders drop. Inhale slowly through your nose for a count of four, feeling your chest and belly expand. Hold that breath for a count of two, then exhale through your mouth for a count of six. Repeat this cycle a few times, noticing the tension easing with each breath.
...that actually helped. like, a little. my chest doesn't feel so tight. thanks.

I’m glad it gave you a bit of relief. Small moments like this can make the bigger challenges feel more manageable. You can use that breathing anytime tension rises. Would you like to add another simple grounding tool to your list?
nah, one thing at a time. i'll stick with the breathing for now. gotta go soon anyway, shift starts in an hour.

That sounds like a good plan—keeping it simple can make it easier to use when you need it. Remember, you can reach out anytime you want to talk or build on these tools. Take care on your shift tonight. Would you like a quick reminder of the breathing steps before you head out?
yeah, actually. could use that. write it down so i can check later?

Sure—here’s a quick version:  

1. Sit comfortably and relax your shoulders.  
2. Inhale through your nose for 4 seconds.  
3. Hold your breath for 2 seconds.  
4. Exhale through your mouth for 6 seconds, repeat as needed.
